In clean and onion architectures, source-code dependencies point inward, so inner layers (entities, use cases) have no knowledge of outer layers (frameworks, UI, database).
Domain entities should be framework-agnostic, depending only on the PHP language and possibly its standard library, with no Doctrine or Symfony imports.
Controllers and Twig templates belong to the presentation (UI/infrastructure) layer, not the business-logic layer; they merely invoke use cases that live in the application or domain layer.
In onion architecture, the domain model (entities and domain logic) forms the innermost core, with all other layers depending inward toward it.
Tools like deptrac analyze class dependencies against configured layer rules and report or fail the build when a forbidden dependency exists.

Clean architecture says use cases should not depend on frameworks or infrastructure like HTTP requests or EntityManager; they should receive plain input data and depend on abstractions such as repository interfaces.
A Repository provides an in-memory-like collection interface for aggregates or entities while abstracting away the underlying persistence mechanism.
In clean architecture, the domain and use cases depend only on abstractions (ports/interfaces), so the database is an outer-layer detail that can be swapped by changing its adapter implementation.

In Domain-Driven Design, an aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit for data changes, with a root entity enforcing consistency; it is not the same as a database table, though it may be persisted across one or more tables.
A Value Object is defined by its attribute values, is immutable, and equality is based on those values rather than object identity.
The aggregate root is the single entity through which all external access and state changes to the aggregate must pass, enforcing its invariants.
In Domain-Driven Design, repositories are defined per aggregate root, since the root is the only entry point for accessing and modifying objects within the aggregate.
In Domain-Driven Design, the ubiquitous language is the shared vocabulary, built from the domain model, used by both developers and domain experts.
The domain (universe) of discourse is the set of objects within which a model's language has a consistent interpretation, and outside which the same expressions can denote different things.
Domain-Driven Design recommends rich domain models where behavior and invariants live in entities and value objects; anemic models with logic pushed into services are considered an anti-pattern.

In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context defines a boundary within which a particular model applies, so the same real-world concept (e.g., a 'Customer') can have different representations and classes in different contexts.
Symfony's DI container instantiates services only when they are first requested, unless a service is explicitly marked as eager or is needed by another service earlier.

PostgreSQL's MVCC means readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers, since readers see a snapshot of committed data while writers create new row versions.
EXPLAIN displays the query's execution plan without actually running the query (unlike EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which executes it).

In PostgreSQL, NULL values are considered distinct from one another, so a UNIQUE constraint allows multiple rows with NULL by default (NULLS NOT DISTINCT is needed to restrict this, in PostgreSQL 15+).
PostgreSQL's string_agg(expression, delimiter) concatenates non-null input values into one string, separated by the given delimiter.
Plain VACUUM marks space from dead tuples as reusable within the table but generally does not return it to the operating system; only VACUUM FULL or similar rewrites do that.
The PARTITION BY clause in an OVER() window definition divides the rows into groups over which the window function is computed.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; non-repeatable reads are prevented starting at REPEATABLE READ (or higher).
PostgreSQL runs each standalone SQL statement in its own implicit transaction, committed automatically unless an explicit transaction block is used.
The COMMIT statement ends the current transaction and makes all of its changes permanent.
UPDATE and DELETE statements with WHERE clauses on indexed columns can locate target rows quickly via the index instead of scanning the whole table.
PostgreSQL supports savepoints, and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the statements executed after that savepoint within the transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports real timing and row counts, whereas plain EXPLAIN only shows the estimated plan without running it.
The pgvector extension adds a vector data type and indexes (IVFFlat and HNSW) for similarity search over embeddings in PostgreSQL.
A partial index contains entries only for table rows that satisfy its WHERE predicate, which makes it smaller and cheaper to maintain.

PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which tracks read/write dependencies with predicate locks and aborts transactions on conflicts rather than locking the rows read.
HTTP status 201 Created indicates the request succeeded and a new resource was created as a result.
HTTP 204 No Content indicates the request succeeded and there is no content in the response body, commonly used after DELETE.
RFC 7231 (section 4.2.2) classifies DELETE as idempotent, meaning repeated identical requests leave the server state the same, although the response status may differ (for example, 204 then 404).
Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a response header sent by the server to tell the browser which origins may read the response; the client sends the Origin header, not this one.
HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests indicates the user has sent too many requests in a given time window, typically exceeding a rate limit.
It is reversed: 4xx status codes indicate client errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type header specifies the MIME type of the body in a request or response.
RFC 5789 states that PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent, whereas PUT is required to be idempotent under RFC 7231.
A plain == comparison can leak timing information, so hash comparisons should use hash_equals() or, better, password_verify().
A session-bound CSRF token generated by the server and validated on state-changing requests like POST is the standard defense against cross-site request forgery.
The Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header enables and defines the Content Security Policy for a page.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, not an authentication protocol; the access token grants access to resources and does not itself identify the user (OpenID Connect adds the identity layer via ID tokens).

XSS is prevented by context-aware output encoding/escaping when rendering data, not merely by validating input before storage, since data can enter the page through many paths and the correct escaping depends on the output context.
The authorization server redirects to the redirect_uri with a 'code' query parameter, which the client then exchanges for an access token at the token endpoint.
Refresh tokens have a longer lifetime than access tokens and are used to obtain new access tokens without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
Salts are stored alongside the hash and are not secret; their purpose is to defeat precomputed rainbow tables, and verification uses the stored salt.
PHPUnit only collects test methods from classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase (or provide a suite() method), so extending TestCase is required.
PHPUnit's setUp() runs before each individual test method, not once before all tests in the class; setUpBeforeClass() is the method that runs once per class.
A PHPUnit data provider supplies multiple argument sets, and the test runs once for each set, not just one.
PHPUnit's expectException() method declares that the test is expected to throw an exception of the given class.
It is the reverse: a stub only returns canned data without verifying calls, while a mock records and verifies which methods were invoked.
PHPUnit 10 and later favor the #[DataProvider] attribute, and the older @dataProvider docblock annotation is deprecated.

PHPUnit's --order-by option with the random value runs tests in random order (also accepts --random-order and --random-order-seed).
